title: Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes
one_liner: A micro-bounty network that pays home inspectors, plumbers and water-heater installers to photograph where the service line enters the basement, with AI classification, so utilities can clear 'unknown material' lines for about $40 each instead of $500-3,000 each.
customer: Mid-size municipal and district water utilities (20k-300k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their published lead service line inventory. The buyer is the utility director or the lead program manager. A secondary payer is the home buyer, who pays about $29 for a 'Lead Line Certificate' add-on at inspection.
problem: Since the lead and copper inventory requirement, every system has had to classify each service line as lead, galvanized-requiring-replacement, non-lead or unknown. Unknowns are a legal and financial liability, and they are hard to shrink. The only sure verification is potholing or excavation, which costs hundreds to thousands of dollars per line. Customer self-ID by mailer gets a response rate of roughly 10-25%. Absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. Utility crews can't look inside private basements, so tens of thousands of unknowns sit in the spreadsheet for years.
solution: A mobile app with a fixed 3-photo protocol: the pipe where it enters the building, a scratch or magnet test close-up, and the meter serial number with the address. A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, PEX, PVC or HDPE, or flags it as unresolved. Humans QA the low-confidence cases. Each submission is geo-verified and tamper-evident, and exports in the format the state inventory portal expects. Inspectors and plumbers earn $15-25 per verified line, and the platform earns the spread. The utility gets a reconciled inventory feed and a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP code. The consumer add-on (inspector-branded certificate, sold to the buyer) pays the inspector while giving the utility free data.
why_now: The first inventories were filed in late 2024, and public analyses showed millions of lines still classified 'unknown'. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements set a 10-year replacement clock that starts around 2027, though federal details keep being revisited and litigated. Several states have their own replacement statutes that don't depend on the federal rule. The $15B in dedicated infrastructure-law lead line money is moving through state revolving funds under spend-down pressure. Vision models are only now accurate enough to classify pipe photos. (Regulatory details are from memory. Verify state acceptance rules before pitching.)
revenue_model: Utilities pay $30-60 per verified line, sold as a per-line contract that fits under small-purchase thresholds. A $10-25k pilot is typical, followed by annual contracts. The consumer-paid certificate ($29) is split with the inspector. Later products are inventory-reconciliation SaaS and an access-agreement workflow for replacement crews.
non_obvious_insight: Utilities think they have a data problem, but they have an eyeballs-in-basements problem. Every home sale (an inspector visits) and every water heater swap (a plumber stands three feet from the service entry) already puts a paid expert next to the exact pipe that matters. Nobody has paid them for a photo yet. Excavation is the wrong tool for a question that visual inspection answers for almost nothing.
first_30_days: Pick one state that accepts documented visual or contractor verification. Pick two utilities in it whose public inventories are more than 40% unknown. Recruit 30 inspectors through local InterNACHI and ASHI chapter meetups and Facebook groups, and pay a launch bonus per photo set. Run a 200-line pilot. Have the utility pothole 30 of those lines as ground truth, then publish the accuracy numbers. Close a $15-25k pilot purchase order with the first utility, using the small-purchase limit that many cities set at $25-50k so no council vote is needed.

title: PFAS Test-Result Exchange for Small Brands
one_liner: A members' data pool where small brands share lab results indexed by supplier, material lot and SKU, so nobody pays $500+ to test the same fabric or coating twice.
customer: Product-compliance managers at small and mid-size apparel, outdoor, cookware, cosmetics, textile and food-packaging brands and importers ($5M-$200M revenue) selling into US states with PFAS product laws and into the EU.
problem: PFAS rules are fragmenting through state product bans and reporting laws, EU packaging limits and a pending EU universal restriction (all unverified in the briefing; re-check current status). Supplier declarations fail because suppliers often do not know what is in their coatings. Testing costs hundreds of dollars per sample, and small brands that buy from the same mills and coaters each test alone. 'PFAS-free' marketing claims also draw class actions.
solution: A neutral cooperative. Members upload lab PDFs, which are parsed automatically and tagged to supplier, mill, material spec and date. The exchange scores confidence per supplier-material ('3 independent labs, 12 samples, all under threshold'), flags outliers, recommends where a new test buys the most certainty per dollar, negotiates group lab rates, and generates the state or EU evidence file. Contributions earn credits.
why_now: State PFAS product deadlines and EU packaging PFAS limits are landing in 2025-26 (background, verify), total-fluorine screening is cheap enough to run routinely, and LLM parsing turns messy lab PDFs into structured data.
revenue_model: Membership of $3-15k/year by revenue tier, pay-per-query for non-contributors, a 10-15% margin on group lab testing, and a paid 'independently verified' badge program.
non_obvious_insight: Declarations fail through ignorance, not malice, so the durable defense is measurement. Measurement is a shared-cost, non-competitive good, like a credit bureau for materials. Antitrust risk is low if the pool holds test data only and never pricing.
first_30_days: Partner with one accredited lab and one trade association (outdoor or apparel). Recruit 10 founding members who contribute 200+ historical lab reports, stand up a spreadsheet-backed MVP with parsed PDFs, and charge a $2.5k founding fee.

title: Pre-Surveyed Superload Corridors for Data Center Freight
one_liner: A subscription library of continuously re-verified main supply routes for 100-400 ton transformer and switchgear moves, so heavy-haul carriers stop paying for a bespoke route survey on the same corridors every time.
customer: Heavy-haul carriers and project-cargo forwarders moving transformers, switchgear and generators to data centers and substations. Secondary buyers are EPC contractors, equipment OEMs and state permit offices.
problem: Every superload needs a route survey covering bridge ratings, turn radii, overhead lines, signals, rail crossings and escort rules. It costs weeks and real money, and it is repeated from scratch for the same handful of corridors from ports and rail heads to the same data-center clusters. Transformer deliveries are project cargo booked years ahead, and the domestic flatbed leg is at its tightest in years. The delay that kills schedules is rarely the bridge. It is the utility that needs six weeks and a bucket-truck crew to lift a line.
solution: Treat major corridors like military main supply routes: classify them once, then re-verify on a cycle. A survey crew captures mobile LiDAR, 360 imagery and pole-height data on a fixed corridor, then builds a route package with go/no-go strip maps and choke-point drawings. Each choke point carries the owner and the lead time to clear it (which utility, how many weeks, what it costs, which county road closures and escort rules apply). Sell annual corridor subscriptions, with an engineer-stamped per-move certification as an add-on. Recruit surveyors from retired combat engineers and route-reconnaissance veterans.
why_now: Data-center buildout is turning transformers into the pacing item. Industry reporting expects annual U.S. transformer demand to rise from roughly 1,500 units today toward 9,000 by 2030, with about 12 GW of capacity announced across roughly 140 projects for 2026 but only about 5 GW under construction. Forwarders now lock in manufacturing slots, ports and heavy-haul routes years ahead, and the trucking leg has a second lead-time problem.
revenue_model: Corridor subscription of about $15-60k a year per carrier per corridor, per-move engineer-certified route stamp of $3-10k, and data licenses to OEMs, developers and forwarders who want pre-clearance before quoting a delivery date.
non_obvious_insight: Route knowledge decays, and reuse is high. A few dozen corridors carry most loads, so a maintained library beats one-off surveys the way a pre-classified main supply route beats a fresh reconnaissance. The value is freshness (last verified date) and the choke-point ownership map, not the imagery. Carriers will trade permission to reuse survey data for a discount on their own move, which funds the first corridors.
first_30_days: Choose one corridor with a live job, such as a Gulf Coast port to a Texas data-center cluster or a feeder route into a Northern Virginia campus. Offer a friendly heavy-haul carrier a discounted survey of its actual move in exchange for the right to reuse the data. Use a rented or $30-40k rig (GNSS, laser pole, 360 camera) and 2 veterans with route-reconnaissance or heavy-haul permit experience. Package the deliverable, then sell corridor #2 to that carrier's competitors and to a transformer OEM's logistics manager.

title: Part-Time Retired Journeymen as Apprentice Supervisors
one_liner: Supervision-as-a-service: retired licensed tradespeople work 2-3 days a week as the supervising journeyman that lets small shops deploy the apprentices and helpers they already have.
customer: 5-25 employee electrical, plumbing and HVAC shops with unlicensed helpers or apprentices, starting in one state with clear ratio and qualifier rules. They pay by the hour.
problem: The headlines say the pipeline is the shortage, but the Gen Z enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage. For many shops the binding constraint is licensed supervision, because ratio rules cap helpers per journeyman. Data-center overtime ($130-170K for journeymen, vendor stat) pulls supervisors off residential work. ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, yet retirees hold exactly the scarce credential and are unused.
solution: A vetted, insured bench of retired journeymen and masters placed part-time in shops as supervising journeyman and mentor. The platform verifies licenses, runs employer-of-record or 1099 structure per state rules, handles workers' comp, and automates the apprenticeship hour logs boards require. Shops book blocks such as Tue-Thu 7-3.
why_now: ABC's 2026 gap of 349K is mostly retirement. Data centers now account for nearly a third of the shortage. Immigration enforcement removes helpers, so shops need to hire and supervise local apprentices fast. Trade-school hype is masking a thin pipeline.
revenue_model: Shops pay about $75-110 per hour billed. The platform keeps 20-25% and the retiree keeps the rest. Add $150-250 per month for hour-logging and compliance software.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not labor, it is supervision minutes, and retirees want 16-hour weeks that no normal employer offers. A supervising journeyman unlocks one or two helpers billing at journeyman-adjacent rates, so shops can pay a premium and still gain margin. Rules vary by state and must be verified before launch.
first_30_days: Pick one trade (electrical) in one state with clear ratio rules. Recruit 15 retirees from union retiree groups and lapsing-license lists. Sign 5 shops with 3+ helpers who are idle or under-deployed. Bill the first hours in week 3.

title: Hardware-Origin Audits for Drones and Robots
one_liner: Teardown-level bill-of-materials and firmware audits that prove what is really inside a 'US-made' drone or robot, sold to small makers, to the public-safety and utility buyers who must prove compliance, and to insurers.
customer: US drone and robot makers with 5-100 employees selling to public safety, utilities, agriculture and federally funded programs. Buyers: county, city and state procurement offices and grant recipients. Insurers and lenders who need 'no covered components' assurance.
problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in Dec 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in Sep 2026 with component tariffs in 2027, and China's export controls cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Buyers must show they bought compliant gear, but suppliers self-declare, rebrand and reroute. Procurement staff cannot inspect a flight controller. After the IEEPA tariff-refund saga, customs origin claims will draw scrutiny. Unitree G1 at about $16k tempts robot buyers into the same problem.
solution: An auditor plus registry. Teardown-level BOM verification (identify chips and modules, firmware and network-callback tests for covered-vendor endpoints, cross-check of supplier declarations and customs documents). It produces a signed origin and compliance dossier per model and lot. A public registry lets procurement staff query a model against state and federal restrictions.
why_now: The FCC action, tariffs and Chinese export controls all landed between Dec 2025 and Sep 2026. Domestic supply is emerging (Amprius won a $75M award for 500 Wh/kg cells), and dozens of new entrants all claim 'American-made'. A number of state laws also restrict agencies from buying Chinese drones (specifics to verify).
revenue_model: $8k-$30k per product audit for makers. $1k-$3k per re-certification on a BOM change. $2k-$5k/yr buyer-side registry subscription for agencies. Lot-level spot-check fees. Referral fees from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: When a ban creates a market, the scarce asset is belief in compliance, not the compliant product. The audit fee is a tax on every new entrant, and buyers fear being embarrassed by an audit finding. Inputs are cheap (a bench, a spectrum analyzer, firmware tooling) and one engineer can produce the first audits. The same dossier doubles as customs-origin evidence.
first_30_days: With maker consent (or from public teardowns), audit 5 currently marketed 'American-made' drones and publish the methodology. Offer three small US makers a $5k pre-audit with a money-back guarantee. Sell 3 full audits at $10k-$15k. Pitch a state public-safety procurement association on the registry.

title: Independent Robot Bake-Off and Acceptance Lab
one_liner: A neutral test cell where warehouse buyers watch robots handle their own SKUs and pallets before signing, with published, verified throughput numbers.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs, grocers and retailers (roughly 50-500k sq ft) evaluating palletizing, picking or humanoid pilots. Robot vendors are a second payer (for certification), and lenders and insurers are a third.
problem: Vendors control the demo. Buyers cannot verify throughput on their own product mix, and pilots eat 6-12 months. Funding is running far ahead of proof: Maven raised a $100M Series A with about 8 robots deployed, Agility booked $1.8M of revenue against a $2.5B SPAC valuation, and early 1X NEO demos were largely teleoperated.
solution: Rent a 20-30k sq ft cell in a logistics hub. Buyers ship 200 pallets or 500 SKUs. Vendors run their robots under a standard protocol. The lab logs picks per hour, error rate, human-intervention minutes, teleop minutes and mean time between failures, then issues a 'Verified Throughput' report. Buyers pay per bake-off, and vendors pay to list certified results and retest after software updates.
why_now: In 2026 procurement teams face a flood of unverifiable claims: about 22k humanoids shipped in H1, nine-figure rounds go to companies with a handful of deployed units, and buyers want outcome pricing. Nobody independent sits between vendors and buyers.
revenue_model: $15-40k per buyer-commissioned bake-off, $25-75k a year per vendor for certification and retests, and data licensing of failure-mode datasets to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's binding constraint is trust in claims, not capability. Vendors will pay for independent verification because their real bottleneck is a 9-12 month sales cycle (compare UL, J.D. Power, Wirecutter). The failure-mode data becomes an asset that insurers, lenders and model developers all want.
first_30_days: Rent demo floor space inside a friendly integrator's or 3PL's idle mezzanine. Sign 2 mid-size 3PLs to paid bake-offs of 3 vendors each, and give vendors a free first test in exchange for the right to publish. Release the public methodology and a first leaderboard of 'intervention minutes per hour'.

title: Wet-Lab Materials Bill-of-Materials Scanner
one_liner: Black Duck for biology: scan a startup's plasmids, cell lines, antibodies and enzymes for license, MTA and patent encumbrances before an investor or acquirer does.
customer: Venture-backed biotechs 6-12 months from a Series B, IPO or M&A, acquirers' diligence teams, university spinouts, and IP counsel.
problem: Materials used freely in academia carry limits in for-profit use: Addgene third-party limited-use label licenses, research-only cell-line licenses, Cas9, base-editor and promoter patents, and MTA restrictions. Nobody inventories a lab's biological dependencies, so surprises surface in diligence and cut price or delay closing. At least 12 funded biotechs were sold for $1B+ in 2026, so acquirer diligence is intense.
solution: Ingest LIMS or Benchling exports, plasmid GenBank files and strain and cell-line lists. Match them against a curated encumbrance database (Addgene label-license data, depositor MTAs, patent sequence claims, vendor terms). Output a risk-ranked report with remediation options (license, replace, design around), continuous scanning as inventory changes, and attorney-reviewed summaries.
why_now: Deal volume is high, LIMS exports are easy, and software license scanning is a well-understood category that buyers already recognize.
revenue_model: $12-40k per scan, $30-100k annual continuous monitoring, and sprint pricing for acquirers' diligence teams.
non_obvious_insight: In software, license scanning is standard. In biology the dependencies are physical, unlisted and cross borders, so no bill of materials exists. One database sells to both sides: acquirers use it to find hidden liabilities, startups use it to fix them cheaply before the deal.
first_30_days: Build scanner v0 for plasmid sequences against about 200 known encumbered parts and labels. Run free scans for 10 startups through the SynBioBeta network and convert 3 to $12-15k audits. Recruit an IP attorney as advisor.

title: Backflow Testers Roll-Up With Portal-Filing Agents
one_liner: Consolidate small backflow-test shops, then use agents to parse city notices, schedule tests and file results in each water utility's portal, turning mandated annual tests into a low-churn route business.
customer: Property managers, restaurants, car washes, medical buildings, HOAs and multifamily owners who must test backflow assemblies annually, and water utilities who benefit from compliance. Retiring tester shops are the sellers.
problem: Most jurisdictions require annual (sometimes more frequent) tests by a certified tester who submits results to the local water purveyor, and portals and forms vary by utility. Owners miss deadlines and get shutoff threats. Testers are solo or small shops using paper. A failed test triggers repairs worth several times the test fee.
solution: Buy small tester shops to build route density. AI ops: an intake agent parses utility letters and portal notices across a manager's whole portfolio, schedules the nearest tester, files results with browser-automation agents, tracks failures and sends repair quotes. Expand into other mandate-locked recurring routes such as fire extinguisher and sprinkler inspection, kitchen hood, cross-connection surveys and enhanced septic O&M.
why_now: Browser and computer-use agents can now reliably operate idiosyncratic municipal portals. Utilities are moving to online-only submission of test results, and owner-testers are aging out.
revenue_model: $75 to $150 per test, $300 to $1,500 per repair or rebuild, plus annual portfolio management fees for property managers.
non_obvious_insight: A regulator creates the demand and portal friction is the moat. Tests are the loss-leader; repairs, replacements and installs after failed tests carry the margin. Any 'city letter, must act' recurring compliance category is underserved by software, because each authority's process is different.
first_30_days: Start as a compliance concierge for 10 property managers at $15 to $25 per device per year, subcontracting the tests to local certified testers. Build the notice parser and one or two portal integrations. After the flow works, buy one tester shop (about $100k to $250k of owner earnings) on seller financing.

title: Keep-the-House Buyout Desk for Divorcing Spouses
one_liner: A divorce-specific mortgage desk that keeps the low-rate first mortgage alive, gets the leaving spouse released, and funds the equity buyout with a small second lien instead of a full high-rate cash-out refinance.
customer: Divorcing homeowners, mostly aged 40 to 65, who want to keep the house. Channels: mediators, divorce attorneys, CDFAs and DIY-divorce platforms.
problem: A divorce decree cannot release a co-borrower from the mortgage. Only a formal assumption with release, which requires servicer underwriting of the keeping spouse, or a refinance can do that. Many conventional loans are not assumable, though a transfer to a spouse under a decree is exempt from due-on-sale, while FHA, VA and USDA loans can be assumed. Servicers often mishandle these requests. Many homeowners hold first mortgages far below today's rates, so a full refinance wrecks affordability and the house gets sold.
solution: Intake on loan type, rate, equity and incomes, then a one-page keep versus sell versus refinance model showing blended-rate math. Then execute the sequence: title transfer under the divorce exemption, an assumption-with-release packet built for the servicer, buyout financing through a partner HELOC or closed-end second lien (or a shared-equity note from the leaving spouse), and suggested decree language for attorneys, such as a buyout-financing contingency and a release deadline.
why_now: Millions of borrowers still hold sub-4% mortgages while current rates are higher, and tappable home equity is large. The share of divorces involving people over 50 keeps growing, and those couples have the most equity. DIY-divorce platforms now produce decrees with no mortgage plan.
revenue_model: A flat $495 to $995 planning fee. Broker compensation of about 1% to 2% on second-lien or HELOC originations (requires an NMLS-licensed loan officer or partner). Licensing to DIY-divorce platforms and mediation firms. Avoid referral fees to attorneys because of fee-splitting rules.
non_obvious_insight: Lawyers treat the house as a property-division problem when it is a loan-portability problem. The low-rate first mortgage is often the most valuable asset in the marriage. Illustratively, keeping $300k at 3% and borrowing $100k at 8.5% blends to about 4.4%, versus about 6.5% on a $400k cash-out refinance, roughly $300 to $400 a month less in payment. Nobody in the divorce process is paid to run that comparison.
first_30_days: Partner with one NMLS-licensed loan officer and two HELOC or second-lien lenders. Publish the calculator and a 'divorce and your mortgage' guide. Offer 5 mediators, divorce attorneys or CDFAs a free house model for their next 10 clients. Process 5 live cases and build servicer-by-servicer playbooks on assumption timelines and release requirements. Then sell the flat-fee plan to DIY-divorce customers.

title: Chaos Testing for Buildings as Code-Required Commissioning
one_liner: An agent that safely actuates a building's HVAC at night, forcing dampers, valves and pumps through scripted step tests, to produce the functional-test evidence that codes require and passive analytics cannot.
customer: Commissioning firms and energy-service companies, and owners of 100k-2M sq ft commercial buildings facing performance standards (NYC Local Law 97, Washington and Denver building performance standards) and California Title 24 acceptance testing.
problem: Passive fault-detection analytics cannot tell 'stuck damper' from 'no demand'. Functional performance tests are still done by hand on clipboards at handover and rarely repeated, so buildings drift into waste. Emissions penalties and code-required acceptance tests raise the stakes, yet commissioning agents are labor-constrained.
solution: Connect through a BACnet or BAS gateway with read/write access. An LLM converts Sequences of Operation (ASHRAE Guideline 36 or project spec PDFs) into bounded test scripts with safety envelopes and automatic rollback. Overnight runs produce pass/fail results with evidence, a deficiency list with estimated savings, and signed test reports for compliance. Re-run quarterly, with operator approval built in.
why_now: BAS gateways and cloud connections are mainstream. LLMs can now parse sequences and generate test logic. Building performance standards, including LL97, are producing real penalties, and utilities pay for measured savings. Commissioning firms cannot hire enough engineers.
revenue_model: $5-15k per building test campaign, $1-3k per month for ongoing quarterly testing, white-label resale through commissioning firms at about 30% margin, and shared-savings deals with ESCOs.
non_obvious_insight: Active probing creates ground-truth labels that passive analytics lack, and the law already requires many of the tests, so automating them cuts a mandatory cost rather than selling a discretionary energy project. Chaos engineering is routine in software but almost unknown in buildings because nobody trusts write access, so the real product is the safety envelope, rollback and operator sign-off, more than the AI.
first_30_days: Partner with two commissioning-authority firms. Agree on five common tests (economizer, VAV minimum flow, chiller staging, sensor cross-checks, pump changeover). Run them on 3 buildings with BACnet access at a fixed fee priced at 40-60% of a manual test, and document the energy findings.

title: PFAS Farm Passport for Food Buyers and Lenders
one_liner: A screening-plus-sampling service that tells dairy co-ops, produce processors and ag lenders which supplier farms carry PFAS risk from sludge spreading or contaminated irrigation water, and certifies the clean ones.
customer: Dairy co-ops, regional produce and hay buyers, private-label sourcing teams and agricultural lenders. The buyer pays for its supplier base, and farms pay for re-verification.
problem: The industry frames PFAS as a 4 ppt tap-water rule, and EPA's proposed delay to 2031 and rescissions seem to give slack. The abrupt financial shock is on farms: biosolids-spread fields and PFAS-laden irrigation or well water (Maine's shut-down farms are the precedent). There is no farm-level limit, so lenders and buyers cannot underwrite.
solution: A 'PFAS Farm Passport'. First, a desktop risk screen from public biosolids-application permits, industrial discharger locations and nearby well data. Second, a targeted sampling protocol (irrigation water, soil, forage, milk) run through a partner lab. Third, a risk tier and a 'verified clean' attestation for buyers and lenders. Fourth, remediation triage (change water source, crop or field use).
why_now: Regulatory loosening pushes risk assessment onto private buyers, who cannot wait for rules. The 2027 monitoring data will make PFAS geography public. Maine-style farm closures have put buyers on notice, and private supplier standards tend to outrun public ones.
revenue_model: $300-800 desktop screen per farm (paid by buyer), $1-3k per sampling round, $100-300k/yr enterprise contracts for processors with 500-2,000 suppliers, and lender portfolio-screening fees.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers fear being caught selling contaminated milk, not violating a tap-water limit. In food supply chains a private standard beats the public rule, so the gap between the EPA rollback and buyer fear is the market.
first_30_days: Choose one region with open biosolids-application records (Michigan, Wisconsin or Maine). Screen 500 farms desktop-only. Give three regional dairy co-ops or processors a free 'top 20 at-risk suppliers' preview, and sell a paid 50-farm sampling pilot.

title: Settlement Back Office for Farm Water Conservation
one_liner: Program administration as a service that enrolls small farms in paid fallowing and conservation programs, verifies acre-feet with satellite evapotranspiration plus meter data, pays within 14 days, and hands the farm's CPA a clean tax packet.
customer: Payers: irrigation districts, state and basin conservation programs, corporate-funded coalitions and cities buying temporary leases, who pay the admin fee. End users: family farms of 50-800 irrigated acres in the Colorado River basin.
problem: The 2027-2036 framework pushes the next cuts onto agriculture, which takes about 70% of the river. Buyers want verified acre-feet at a price per acre-foot. Farmers want simple metering and fast payment, and fear that fallowing weakens their water right. Amazon's $20M ($32M raised toward a $100M goal) shows demand with no settlement layer. Programs run on spreadsheets and site visits, so small farms wait months and mis-report the income.
solution: A portal that enrolls farms and sets a consumptive-use baseline from public field-scale ET data, pump-power meter data and the farm's own records. Local crop advisors are paid per visit to verify. Contract templates carry a 'right-protection' letter agreed with the state water agency. ACH payment in 14 days. Automatic W-9 and 1099 handling, plus a tax and books packet on income timing and conservation-payment treatment for the farm's CPA. Funders get an audit-ready acre-foot ledger.
why_now: Interior issued the Record of Decision in Aug 2026 with Powell and Mead at about 36% of capacity. 95% of the basin is in drought. Corporate and public conservation money is arriving with no back office. Free satellite ET data and cheap power-meter telemetry now make remote verification credible, and LLMs make program-specific agreements and tax packets cheap.
revenue_model: 3-5% of disbursed funds as a program admin fee. $150 per farm onboarding fee, paid by the program. Later, a spread on instant-pay float. A $100M coalition goal at 4% is about $4M of admin revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Water markets fail at settlement and trust, not price discovery. A farmer will fallow if he is paid in weeks and his water right is legally shielded. The winning product is paperwork plus a legal shield letter plus a tax packet, not a marketplace. The customer who pays is the funder who would otherwise have to staff a program office.
first_30_days: Approach 3 irrigation districts or NGOs running conservation pilots and offer to administer 20-40 farms for a flat pilot fee. Build the enrollment form, an ET baseline report from public data and ACH payout in 30 days. Sign an LOI with one coalition partner. Recruit an agricultural CPA and a water attorney as advisers to draft the shield-letter approach.

title: A Suable LLC With Reserves for Every Agent
one_liner: Mass-produced, series-LLC legal wrappers that give each paid agent a registered agent for service of process, a capital reserve, and tax handling, so counterparties have someone to sue.
customer: Indie developers and small studios monetizing paid agents, MCP servers and pay-per-call endpoints (they pay). Enterprise buyers and buying agents use the registry for free. Later, enterprises that want internal agents to contract externally without exposing the parent company.
problem: An agent cannot be sued, hold a bank account or be a contract party. A buyer's counsel asks 'who is my counterparty?' and the honest answer is a 22-year-old with a Discord handle. Sellers, meanwhile, face personal liability and VAT/sales-tax obligations across dozens of jurisdictions from micro-sales made without any human checkout.
solution: One low-cost Delaware or Wyoming series-LLC cell per agent, created in batch: registered agent, EIN, bank or stablecoin account, and a mandatory reserve (say $500-5,000) held in T-bills. The agent's public key is registered so any counterparty can resolve key to entity to reserve balance to claims history. Buying agents can enforce a rule such as 'reserve at least 20x order size'. An embedded merchant-of-record partner handles VAT and sales tax, and an optional insurance rider covers errors.
why_now: x402-style stablecoin micro-payments let agents sell without any human checkout. Legal commentators in 2026 are publishing playbooks for wrapping autonomous agents in LLCs (for example Aaron Wright's essay on the agent's legal body and Ledger's work on registered AI entities). Regimes such as California's have made 'the AI did it' no defense, so buyers now want a named responsible entity.
revenue_model: $49 per agent per month plus $99 formation fee, yield on pooled reserves (roughly 4% on float), 1% merchant-of-record fee, and insurance commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Identity is the wrong primitive. Strangers trust each other when the counterparty has something to lose and somewhere a summons can be served, which is exactly what corporations were invented to provide. The reserve is the product and the reputation score is a byproduct. Caveat: veil-piercing and principal liability still apply, so the product must be candid that it makes agents serviceable and collateralized, not judgment-proof.
first_30_days: Partner with a registered-agent firm and one series-LLC attorney. Offer 50 founding 'agent cells' to MCP and paid-endpoint developers via developer communities and X. Handle paperwork in manual batches. Validate demand by getting two enterprise buyers to say they will only purchase from agents with a registered entity and reserve.

title: Fee-Free Hire Receipts for Migrant Workers
one_liner: A worker-held credential proving a migrant was recruited without fees and paid as contracted, sold to suppliers and brands that must prove no forced labour, and portable to the worker's next job.
customer: Tier-1 suppliers and their EU-facing brand buyers in electronics, garments, construction, hospitality and palm oil. Ethical recruitment agencies are a channel, and the worker is the holder.
problem: From 14 December 2027 the EU Forced Labour Regulation bans products made with forced labour, and importers must prove a negative. Audits are sampled snapshots that are easy to game. Workers in corridors such as Nepal to Malaysia or the Philippines to the Gulf often pay illegal recruitment fees that create debt bondage, and they leave with no portable record of employment or skills.
solution: A WhatsApp-first Hire Receipt. At contract signing the worker gets a signed record of recruiter, employer, wage, contract terms and fees paid (zero, or reimbursed). On arrival there is a passport-custody check, then monthly wage-receipt confirmations. Short translated voice check-ins provide independent verification. The worker holds the credential and shares it on consent with employers and brands, which see aggregate dashboards. Over time it accrues employment history and endorsements usable for the next placement or a remittance-backed loan.
why_now: Law firms published compliance roadmaps for the regulation in September 2026, and brands are starting to build supplier evidence programs 15 months before enforcement. Recruitment-fee evidence is the hardest part to get, and no one holds it continuously.
revenue_model: $10-25 per hire paid by the employer or brand, per-site dashboard subscriptions, and placement referral fees from ethical recruiters later.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance buyers must prove a negative, and only worker-side records can do that. Audits fail because they sample, while a worker-held receipt makes evidence continuous, cheaper and self-enforcing. Because the same credential improves the worker's mobility, the worker's incentives align with the buyer's.
first_30_days: Partner with two ethical recruiters in one corridor and one EU-facing supplier. Pilot for 200 hires using a WhatsApp bot rather than an app. Charge a $5k pilot fee plus a per-hire fee, and write up the evidence pack in the format a brand's compliance team will accept.

title: Data Act Unlock for Hotel Connected Equipment
one_liner: Use the EU Data Act's user-access rights to pull hotels' own data out of locked vendor clouds (HVAC, locks, laundry, elevators) into an energy and maintenance ledger that third-party service firms can plug into.
customer: EU independent hotel groups and management companies with 5-50 properties, plus independent HVAC, elevator and kitchen-equipment service firms and energy-optimization vendors that want the data.
problem: After the 2026 Hormuz energy shock, hotel energy costs have been repriced sharply. The data from a hotel's connected thermostats, HVAC, locks, laundry and elevators is trapped in manufacturers' clouds, resold as premium dashboards or API fees. A mixed-brand group cannot build a unified view, and independent maintenance firms cannot diagnose without OEM tools.
solution: Since Sep 2025 the Data Act has let users demand the data generated by connected products and have it shared with a third party they choose (free to the user, on my reading, so verify). New products must offer access by design from 12 Sep 2026. The service is a request desk (letter templates, deadline tracking per OEM, escalation to the national authority) plus connectors that load the data into a property energy and asset ledger, with consent logs for designated recipients.
why_now: The Sep 2026 design-by-default date has just passed and vendors are unprepared, so early requests set the precedents. Energy-cost pain makes the hotel side motivated. The brief also shows small hardware makers scrambling with Data Act and CRA duties, so vendors are stretched.
revenue_model: About EUR 200 per property per month, 10-15% of verified energy savings, and onboarding fees paid by service firms and optimizers who become designated recipients.
non_obvious_insight: Hotels are among the largest accidental 'users' under the Data Act, with dozens of connected products per building, and nobody has told them. The law turns vendor lock-in into a right, the way GDPR created a market for data-subject-request services.
first_30_days: Sign one 10-property group for a flat EUR 1,500 'Data Act audit plus first requests'. Inventory its connected assets, send about 20 access requests across 5 OEMs, and document responses and escalations. Then sell the same audit to 4 more groups and pitch one independent service firm as a designated recipient.

title: MFP Cash Bridge for Independent Pharmacies
one_liner: Reconciliation plus short-term financing for the cash gap independent pharmacies now carry between dispensing at Medicare's negotiated price and getting the manufacturer refund.
customer: Independent pharmacy owners (about 18,000 US stores) with heavy Medicare Part D volume, who are being asked to float thousands of dollars a week.
problem: The first ten Medicare-negotiated 'maximum fair prices' took effect January 1, 2026. Pharmacies buy at wholesale acquisition cost, dispense at the lower MFP and are refunded later through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator, with refunds due within 14 days but the clock starting only when manufacturers receive the data. An analysis for NCPA estimated weekly cash-flow shortfalls above $10K per pharmacy, and a member survey found over 90% of independents are considering not stocking or have stopped stocking one or more of the drugs.
solution: Step one is software: read pharmacy-management system exports and MTF remittance data, reconcile every MFP claim against refunds received, flag underpayments and late refunds, and forecast next week's cash gap. Step two is an advance product: fund verified pending MFP refunds at a small fee, repaid automatically when the MTF payment lands.
why_now: MFP has been live since January 2026, and cash-flow strain is documented. The second negotiation cycle, effective January 2027, adds 15 more drugs (including semaglutide products), so volume and float will grow sharply. Independent pharmacies are already squeezed by PBM reimbursement and store closures, and wholesalers and PBMs have little incentive to solve this.
revenue_model: $149-299 per pharmacy per month for reconciliation and alerts. 0.5-1.5% fee per advance, with a short 14-30 day duration. Warehouse-line financing spread as volume grows.
non_obvious_insight: This is receivables finance in disguise. Refunds owed by big manufacturers through a federal facilitator are among the best-quality, most verifiable small-business receivables in healthcare. The reconciliation software is the underwriting engine, so a small team can start with software, prove default rates are near zero, and then raise a cheap credit line. Being the trusted data layer also positions you for the 2027 and 2028 waves.
first_30_days: Partner with a state pharmacy association or NCPA-affiliated buying group. Recruit 10-15 pharmacies and ingest exports from PioneerRx, Rx30 or QS/1. Sell a $149/month MFP reconciliation dashboard that finds unpaid refunds. Run a free 'cash gap audit' to generate leads. After 60-90 days of clean data, approach a specialty lender for a small advance pilot.

title: Real-Pixel Blink Fixer for Family Formals
one_liner: A Lightroom/Photoshop plugin that turns a 5-frame burst of the 30-person family formal into one frame where every set of eyes is open, using only real pixels from the burst and no generated faces.
customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers (roughly 100k in the US), paying $29-49/mo or about $2 per composite. Later extension: school, team, church and corporate group-portrait photographers.
problem: Family formals are the 20-40 minute block of the day that grandparents care about most. They are also mathematically hostile. If each person has their eyes closed about 8% of the time, a 30-person frame has under a 10% chance of everyone being open, before counting people who look away or squint. So the delivered frame is nearly always a compromise or a composite. Photographers either hand-swap heads in Photoshop (20-40 minutes per group, or $15-40 per image if outsourced), ship the frame with the blinker, or use generative fill. Generative fill invents a face, which is a betrayal when the face is a grandfather who won't be there in two years.
solution: Drop in the formals folder. The tool groups frames into bursts, aligns them (people shift between frames), scores each person's face for eyes open, smile, gaze and sharpness, picks the best patch per person, and blends with seam-aware masks. The output is a layered PSD so the photographer can override any face in one click. The pitch is a strict 'zero generative pixels' guarantee. A second mode is a shoot-time phone companion that says 'frame 3 has 2 blinkers, shoot one more' so bursts are captured with enough variety. The wedge is batch mode for formals only, not a full editor.
why_now: Google's Best Take (Pixel 8, 2023) taught consumers to expect a merged best-expression group photo. Photographers already pay monthly for AI culling and editing, so AI tooling is normal spend in this trade. Adobe's own face-swap route leans on generative fill, which many pros distrust for client faces. On-device face-landmark and eye-state models are now cheap and accurate enough to run locally on a laptop. Searches in Sept 2026 found only manual Photoshop tutorials for this, not a dedicated automated burst-composite product.
revenue_model: Subscription of $29/mo for solo shooters or $2 per composite credit with monthly bundles. Studio plans at $79/mo. Optional white-label API for gallery platforms (Pic-Time, ShootProof-type) later.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody outside the trade realizes that a truly 'perfect' 30-person frame almost never exists in a single exposure, so every delivered formal is quietly a fix or a compromise. The fix that matters is provenance: the people who print the formals at 16x20 are the elderly relatives, and they will notice an AI-invented face on Grandpa. 'Real pixels only' is the actual feature, not the face-swapping.
first_30_days: Build against Lightroom Classic/Photoshop with open-source face-landmark models. Ask 20 photographers in Facebook groups and r/WeddingPhotography to send 3 old formals bursts from past weddings (every working shooter has hundreds sitting in archives). Return composites in 24 hours with before/after slider pages. First 10 composites free, then $2 each via Stripe. Post the before/afters and blink-probability math in photographer communities. Goal is 30 paying studios and one gallery-platform partnership conversation by day 90.

title: Rare Blood Group Assay Foundry
one_liner: Turn each newly recognized blood-group gene into research-use genotyping controls and panels for reference labs, starting with the MAL deletions that define AnWj-negative blood.
customer: Immunohematology reference labs, rare-donor programs and blood centers. Blood-group genotyping platform vendors that want to add content are a second buyer.
problem: AnWj-negative patients, over 99.9% of people are AnWj-positive, can form antibodies against AnWj and risk serious transfusion reactions from ordinary units, and compatible donors are 'extraordinarily difficult' to find. Antibody testing finds the patients but cannot identify rare genetic carriers or donors. Volumes are too small for large diagnostics companies to prioritize.
solution: A small molecular-biology team designs, validates and sells RUO kits: synthetic positive-control DNA for the published MAL deletions, primer and probe sets, and a small validation panel. It then repeats the process for each new ISBT system or rare antigen as the genes are published. It also licenses content to genotyping platform vendors and offers a sample-testing service for rare-donor registries.
why_now: MAL was formally recognized as ISBT blood group system 047 in 2026, and the authors say genotyping tests 'can potentially be incorporated into existing blood group genotyping systems.' Nobody has yet turned the finding into a commercial assay. Cheap gene synthesis and long-read or targeted sequencing make a low-volume, high-value control kit practical for a small team.
revenue_model: RUO control and primer kits at roughly $500-2,000 each, per-sample testing fees for registries, and content-licensing or royalty deals with platform vendors. Later, a CLIA or LDT lab service.
non_obvious_insight: Every new blood-group gene discovery creates a diagnostic gap that big vendors ignore because volume is tiny, and the 47th ISBT system was only just recognized. The NHS Blood and Transplant discovery took nearly 20 years and states that serological testing 'cannot identify rare genetic cases without genetic sequencing' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260918024828.htm; Blood 2024, DOI 10.1182/blood.2024025099). A repeatable foundry that converts each new ISBT gene into a control kit captures a stream of these gaps. Rare-donor matching is a high-willingness-to-pay niche because a single unmatched patient can cost a hospital far more than a kit.
first_30_days: Design gBlock-style synthetic controls for the MAL deletion alleles reported in the Blood paper and validate them on public or donated DNA. Contact the NHS Blood and Transplant IBGRL, the American Rare Donor Program and 5-10 US and EU reference labs to trial the RUO kit. Line up a second gene from the recent ISBT additions. Pitch two platform vendors on a content deal.

title: Payer Offset and Recoupment Radar
one_liner: Reconstruct the silent payer clawbacks buried in the 835 provider-level adjustment segment, then dispute the ones that lack notice or exceed state look-back limits.
customer: Community and mid-size hospitals, physician groups and MSOs, and RCM outsourcers who want a recovery line item. SaaS at $1-3k/month, or 15-25% of reversed recoupments.
problem: Payers increasingly claw money back by netting it inside the electronic remittance (835) PLB provider-level balance segment, or by short-paying unrelated claims. These adjustments carry cryptic reason codes and no patient or claim detail. Cash posters drop them into a suspense or 'other adjustment' account, or write them off. The overpayment letters that justify them arrive by mail, fax or random emails and are never matched. Many states cap retroactive recoupment look-back windows and require claim-level notice, but no one checks whether the payer complied.
solution: Ingest 12-24 months of 835s and the payer's overpayment and audit letters (PDF/email/fax OCR). Rebuild every offset to claim level. Flag recoupments with no valid notice, past the state or contract look-back, duplicating a prior recoupment, or hitting claims already appealed. Generate dispute letters and track outcomes. A payer scorecard shows clawback dollars per $1M paid, which gives the CFO leverage at contract renewal.
why_now: Payer payment-integrity programs are scaling with AI-driven post-payment audits and coding-policy downcodes. Medicare Advantage audit pressure is rising. Hospitals staffed thin after the 2025-26 Medicaid and margin squeeze cannot chase each offset by hand. Post-payment recoupment is the fastest-growing part of the denial problem and the least instrumented.
revenue_model: Contingency 15-25% of recoupments reversed, or $1-3k/month per facility for monitoring plus a $5-10k onboarding audit. Payer scorecards can be sold to hospital associations.
non_obvious_insight: Denial management tools watch denied claims. Recoupments are not denied claims. They are negative dollars in the remit file that nobody owns. Only cash posters see them and they are told to just post them. In a typical mid-size hospital these unmatched offsets total mid-six to seven figures a year, and dispute success is highest exactly where the payer skipped required notice. The data is already sitting in files the hospital owns.
first_30_days: Ask 5 friendly hospital and group cash-posting managers for 12 months of 835s (clearinghouses can export them), which requires only a BAA. Write a parser for the PLB segments (about a week of work) and produce a 'recoupment leakage report' showing unmatched offset dollars per payer. Use the number to sign 2 contingency pilots, and build the letter-matching module on real customer data.

title: Flat-Fee Estate Close-Out Pods for Middle-Class Heirs
one_liner: A retired probate attorney supervises 2-3 junior associates and an AI workflow to close $200K-$2M estates for a flat fee, filling the gap between a $400/hr attorney and nothing while giving locked-out grads a paid apprenticeship.
customer: Executors and heirs of middle-class estates (a house plus retirement accounts), often a grieving widow or an adult child. Channels: funeral homes, hospice social workers, credit unions and elder-law referral networks. Flat fee of about $3,500-6,500.
problem: Wealth managers chase the top 2% of households who hold $62T of the wealth transfer. Middle-class estates get either a $400/hr lawyer or an overwhelmed amateur executor, and probate takes 9-18 months (unverified practitioner claim). Online will sellers treat probate as an add-on. Meanwhile entry-level paralegal, analyst and ops roles that used to train juniors are vanishing (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend).
solution: A 'pod' is one supervising attorney (owning the firm, or operating in a jurisdiction that allows non-lawyer ownership such as Arizona ABS or the Utah sandbox), 2-3 estate associates (laid-off analysts, HR, bank-ops people or grads), and AI workflows for asset discovery, creditor notices, date-of-death valuations, account-closure kits and the final accounting. Each pod runs about 25 estates at once. The heir gets one coordinator, a weekly 15-minute call and one checklist. Associates keep a verifiable log of completed estate steps that ladders to paralegal or licensed-paraprofessional status (AZ, UT, WA, OR, MN).
why_now: Deaths are flat (3.07M in 2024) but dollars per estate are rising, and the first wave of transfers is spousal (about $40T heads to widowed women). AI now handles document drudgery well enough to cut hours per estate from a couple hundred to a few dozen, which turns a not-worth-a-lawyer's-time market into a viable flat-fee product. State regulatory sandboxes are more open to new legal service models than ever.
revenue_model: Flat fee, median about $3,900 with tiers by complexity and state. Target 60%+ gross margin at 25 concurrent estates per pod. Channel partners get flat, bar-compliant marketing fees or co-branded membership benefits (not per-referral fees, which most states bar for lawyers).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in estates is not legal knowledge. It is 100-200 hours of tedious, deadline-driven admin that nobody will pay $400/hr for and no algorithm can be trusted with alone. AI collapses the hours enough to make flat pricing work, and the supervised junior is the feature, not a cost, because employers now refuse to train them.
first_30_days: Sign one retired probate attorney in one county (probate is local). Hire two laid-off analysts. Get 3 funeral homes and 2 hospice social-work teams to hand out a one-page 'first 30 days after a death' checklist with a booking link. Price at $3,900, run 10 estates in 90 days on a manual playbook, then automate the steps that repeat.

title: Idle-Still Co-Packing for Zero-Proof Brands
one_liner: Turn distilleries' idle stills and bottling lines into contract capacity for dealcoholized and botanical spirit brands.
customer: Craft and mid-size distilleries with underused capacity, and zero-proof beverage brands that need production.
problem: US spirits sales fell 15.4% and Diageo's US tequila fell 23% as GLP-1 use spreads, leaving distilleries with fixed costs and empty lines.
solution: A capacity broker and operations layer that matches idle distilleries to zero-proof and functional-tonic brands, handles TTB and formulation paperwork, and standardizes QA and scheduling.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is now visibly cutting alcohol volumes, and the non-alcoholic segment is growing but short of contract capacity with spirit-grade distillation.
revenue_model: 10-15% take on co-pack contracts plus fees for compliance and formulation services.
non_obvious_insight: The first casualties of GLP-1 in beverages are asset-heavy distillers, whose stills are worth more as co-packers to the segment that is replacing them. Grain and agave growers downstream are the next to feel it.
first_30_days: Interview 20 distilleries about idle capacity, line up 5 zero-proof brands with pending production needs, and run one paid pilot batch with a partner distillery.

title: Hours Wallet for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-first tool that proves 80 hours or $580 a month of work for gig and cash earners, paid by Medicaid plans and clinics that lose money when members drop off.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans, FQHCs and hospital financial-counseling teams paying per enrolled or retained member. Users: adults 19-64 in the Medicaid expansion group with irregular income (gig, seasonal, cash, self-employed).
problem: The CMS interim final rule (June 1, 2026) requires about 43 states plus DC to enforce 80 hours per month of work, service or school, or at least $580 per month of earnings, by January 1, 2027, at application and renewal. If compliance cannot be verified the person gets only 30 calendar days to prove it. Proof means pay stubs and letters from employers or volunteer organizations. Arkansas's 2018 requirement cost 18,000 people coverage for failing to meet work or reporting rules.
solution: SMS or WhatsApp-first app that (a) connects gig-platform exports or bank deposits to test the $580 income alternative, (b) sends one-tap timestamped attestation links to a boss, food-bank coordinator or volunteer supervisor, (c) auto-formats the state's monthly report and files it, (d) alerts the member before the 30-day cure window closes, and (e) screens for exemptions such as parents or caretakers of children under 14 and disability. It gives the payer a dashboard of at-risk members.
why_now: The federal rule is final as of June 2026 and states must be live by January 1, 2027 (some earlier, with Nebraska reportedly starting May 1, 2026). Self-attestation is only allowed for 2027, after which documentation is required, so 2027 is the last cheap window to build a member base and data habit before documentation hardens.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month or success fee per retained member from MCOs and FQHCs (about $3-$10/member/month or a bounty per successful renewal), with a free tier for members; secondary revenue from employer-attestation seats for staffing and home-care agencies.
non_obvious_insight: States must first use payroll and other data to verify compliance, which leaves the residual, hardest population (cash, gig and self-employed workers) exactly where a proof tool is needed. Payers, not members, have the money, because each lost member is lost capitation revenue. The CMS rule text (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicaid-community-engagement-requirement-certain-individuals-interim-final-rule-comment-period-cms) gives the $580 alternative, 30-day cure period and exemptions, and KFF's data brief cites the 18,000 Arkansas coverage losses (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/issue-brief/understanding-the-intersection-of-medicaid-and-work-what-does-the-data-say/). Reddit was unreachable, so the r/personalfinance and r/legaladvice 'how do I prove my hours?' demand is forecast from the rule and explainers rather than quoted threads.
first_30_days: Build the $580 income test and attestation-link flow for Nebraska (reportedly already live) plus one January 2027 state. Approach 2 FQHCs and one regional MCO or hospital financial counseling team for a free pilot, and give the tool free to food banks and legal-aid groups as distribution. Aim for 200 pilot members, then convert the clinics to a per-member fee with retained-coverage data as the proof.

title: Texted Pond-Algae and Forage-Poison Alerts for Ranchers
one_liner: Satellite imagery plus weather models watch every stock pond and frost-stressed sorghum field for the handful of killers that wipe out cattle in hours, then text the rancher and route the case to the vet.
customer: Ranchers and horse owners with ponds ($99-249 per year per operation). Bulk channels that pay: rural vet practices offering it as a client service, co-ops and feed dealers bundling it, livestock insurers and county extension programs (via grants) that want loss prevention.
problem: Every late summer and fall vets see clusters of cattle 'found dead' near stock ponds. Blue-green algae toxins kill within hours with no antidote, frost or drought-stunted sudangrass, johnsongrass and sorghum release prussic acid, and nitrates spike after a drought-breaking rain. Ranchers blame lightning, necropsy is rare, and the toxin is gone by the time a lab looks, so the losses are invisible in every statistic and nobody sells prevention. Existing satellite bloom tools target regulators and water bodies over about 1 square kilometer, not one-acre stock ponds.
solution: The rancher texts a location pin or uploads pasture boundaries. The service pulls free Sentinel-2 imagery (10 m resolution, roughly 5-day revisit), runs an open-source small-water-body cyanobacteria model (CyFi from the NASA/NOAA-backed research effort), layers local weather (frost forecast, rainfall after drought) and the forage type, and sends plain SMS: 'Pond in Pasture 4: bloom risk HIGH. Move cattle or run a trough. Your vet is Dr. X.' A one-tap 'I'm worried' reply routes a call to the vet's practice, which bills the visit. Vet-confirmed poisonings feed back to train the model, and later the product adds nitrate, ergot and heat-stress alerts.
why_now: Free 10 m satellite feeds, open ML models for small waterbodies and cheap cloud compute mean a two-person team can now do what used to need a research lab. Hotter summers and drought-then-flood cycles are raising bloom and forage-toxin risk, and with cows and bred heifers worth $3,000+ a five-head loss ($15K+) costs far more than the yearly subscription. Frost season (prussic acid) and late-season blooms are happening right now.
revenue_model: $149 per year per operation for unlimited ponds and pastures, a vet-channel wholesale price of about $2-3 per client per month with the practice keeping the resale margin plus referral visits, co-op bulk licenses, and loss-control contracts with mortality insurers who discount premiums for enrolled ranches.
non_obvious_insight: The rancher will never buy 'algae monitoring', but they will buy 'don't lose your cows'. Vets know that unexplained sudden-death clusters near ponds in August through October are dominated by cyanotoxins and forage toxicities, and that prevention (switch water, delay grazing) is trivial if the warning arrives before the herd does. Each vet-confirmed case is proprietary ground truth that public tools do not have, so accuracy compounds with every season.
first_30_days: Pilot with 20 ranches around 3 vet practices. Run CyFi plus Sentinel-2 on their ponds, and ground-truth flagged ponds with $30 cyanotoxin test strips and vet photos. Sell a $99 season pass through each vet's client newsletter and county extension agents, and time the launch for this fall's frost and late-bloom season. Record every alert, false positive and vet-confirmed case as the training and sales evidence for next summer.

title: Trust Oracle for Rental Listings and Agents
one_liner: An API that answers whether a vacation rental exists, is legally registered and is controlled by the host, so payment firms, insurers and AI booking agents can refuse scams.
customer: Payment providers handling travel, travel insurers, villa-rental agencies and AI trip-agent developers, later consumers via a plug-in.
problem: AI-generated photos and cloned listings fuel rental fraud, and agents will soon book unattended. The EU short-term rental regulation requires registration numbers from May 2026, but there is no cross-border way to verify them and each registry differs. Bans (Barcelona 2028, Palma) will also see illegal listings delisted at the last minute, stranding guests.
solution: Aggregate public registries (Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, France, NYC and others), geocode the address and match it to satellite and street imagery, reverse-search photos and detect duplicates. Return a verified, unverified or unregistered verdict with evidence in under two seconds, as an API and an agent tool.
why_now: Registry numbers make 'is it legal' a lookup for the first time, agentic booking needs automated trust, and AI imagery has broken manual checks. Enforcement is rising (Spain's USD 75M fine on Airbnb).
revenue_model: USD 0.05-0.50 per check, USD 2-10K per month enterprise plans, and a share of insurer premiums saved.
non_obvious_insight: Registration numbers convert legality from opinion into data, and agents cannot get a bad feeling about a listing. Whoever builds the legality and fraud graph first becomes infrastructure for every automated booking flow.
first_30_days: Build for Spain, Italy and Portugal using public registers. Offer a free check widget to villa agencies, and backtest known scam cases to pitch two travel-insurer fraud teams.

title: Audit-Proof Family Night in a Box
one_liner: Fixed-price, compliance-packaged family engagement events for Title I schools, paid from the federally required parent-engagement set-aside, with the monitoring binder as the real product.
customer: District Title I coordinators and Title I principals. The money comes from the ESSA parent and family engagement reserve, which is 1 percent of Title I for districts above the size threshold, and most of it must go to schools.
problem: That money is earmarked but scary to spend. Principals fear audit findings over food, childcare, transport, interpreters and incentives, because each has 'necessary and reasonable' tests and must tie back to the district's engagement policy and the school-parent compact. Events get thin turnout of 20 to 30 percent of families. Principals end up buying pizza with sketchy funds, or the money sits unspent until spring.
solution: A fully produced event in a box. It is built around students performing or presenting, and includes a dinner from a local caterer, on-site childcare, ride vouchers, live interpreters and a personal invitation call script. Every event ships with a pre-vetted allowable-cost memo, an agenda tied to the compact and policy, QR sign-in, a parent needs survey, an evaluation report and a monitoring-ready binder generated automatically. Packages are $4.5k to $9k per event, with annual bundles for a district.
why_now: After the July 2025 federal funding freeze scare and post-ESSER budget cuts, coordinators are under pressure to spend every Title I dollar on time and defensibly. Chronic absenteeism has stuck near one in four students, and family engagement is the best-evidenced lever schools have left. States are also stepping up monitoring of federal-funds documentation.
revenue_model: Per-event fixed fee ($4.5k to $9k), annual multi-event contracts ($25k to $60k per school), and a district-wide compliance template license.
non_obvious_insight: Turnout comes from four things nobody bundles: kids on stage, food, childcare in the building, and a personal call from a known adult. The real blocker is not attendance. It is the principal's fear of an audit finding, so the binder is what they are buying and the event is only the delivery vehicle. Vendors that sell 'parent engagement software' miss this because the software cannot make an allowable-cost decision.
first_30_days: Read one state's Title I monitoring protocol and write a two-page allowable-cost memo. Get two Title I coordinators to comment on it and agree to a template. Pitch 5 principals you know, and run 3 pilot events at cost with a local caterer and a bilingual emcee. Capture turnout data versus the school's usual events. Turn the paperwork into a reusable binder generator.
